morningLine: Epyx goes for gold, Amiga approaches the starting line, and the adventure game puts on a hardback cover.

lead.headline: Summer Games II and Winter Games headline the post-CES games slate
lead.dek: Epyx adds a second summer contest and a winter programme as Lucasfilm adventures line up behind the sports crowd.
body: The home computer is heading back to the stadium. Reporting from the Chicago Summer Consumer Electronics Show, Popular Computing Weekly’s June 13–19 edition puts Epyx’s Summer Games II and Winter Games at the front of a busy games slate. The show took place June 2–5; the news reaching readers this week is a preview of the months ahead.

Summer Games II widens the programme to rowing, triple jump, javelin, high jump, fencing, cycling, kayak canoeing and show jumping. Epyx says the original Summer Games has sold more than 200,000 copies in the United States. The follow-up is promised there for summer, not certified as on sale this week.

Winter Games is pencilled in for autumn. Its proposed events include skiing, ski jump, biathlon, figure skating, freestyle skating and bobsleigh. The change of season gives Epyx a second sporting programme while keeping the emphasis on a varied collection of events.

The same report adds two Lucasfilm adventures to Epyx’s plans: The Eidolon, with cavern exploration aboard a nineteenth-century machine, and Koronis Rift, concerned with recovering ancient weapons. Activision, meanwhile, has announced a Lucasfilm publishing agreement outside North America, with Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus expected in Europe and Australia this summer. These remain announced plans rather than a timetable of verified retail arrivals.

stories.headline: Amiga preview raises the stakes against Atari and Macintosh
body: Commodore’s coming Amiga is becoming the machine to watch. Popular Computing Weekly forecasts an American launch on July 18 and describes a $1,995 package with monitor and disk drive. These are the magazine’s prelaunch expectations, not a completed launch or a settled shop price.

The report describes a Motorola 68000, 256K of RAM expandable to 512K, a mouse-operated Intuition interface and Amiga-DOS. Its graphics account ranges from 320 by 200 to 640 by 400, with differing colour counts and a palette reaching 4,096 colours. Four sound channels add to the entertainment promise.

The British timetable looks longer: Commodore UK general manager Nick Bessey expects no British announcement before January. Entertainment, education and home business are all in the pitch, but the immediate story is anticipation, with Atari and Macintosh providing the competitive backdrop.

stories.headline: Amstrad aims its 128K CPC at the American home
body: Amstrad is aiming the CPC 6128 at American homes this autumn. The June 13–19 Popular Computing Weekly reports the preceding CES announcement, quoting $699 with a green monitor and $799 with a colour monitor. The prices belong to an announced package, not a verified sale this week.

The Z80 machine switches between two 64K memory banks and includes a three-inch disk drive. The report describes software compatibility upward from the CPC 464 and CPC 664, giving the proposed American customer an existing software family rather than an entirely empty shelf.

Chicago-based Indescomp Inc is the distributor. Established in January by Madrid’s Indescomp SA, it is presented as a separate commercial venture: Amstrad supplies the machines, rather than taking a financial partnership in the project.

stories.headline: Poet Robert Pinsky takes the text adventure into the electronic novel
body: The electronic novel is borrowing more than a name from the book trade. June’s COMPUTE!’s Gazette profiles poet Robert Pinsky and Synapse’s Mindwheel for the Commodore 64, placing literary authorship beside the familiar machinery of the text adventure.

Synapse has looked beyond conventional game development for writers who can expand the imaginative territory of interactive fiction. The feature also discusses Douglas Adams and The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, and the balance between pictures and the memory left for vocabulary and sophisticated parsing.

The packaging makes the literary ambition tangible: these electronic novels arrive as hardback books with a disk at the back, and information in the printed volume is needed to play. This is June feature coverage of the form, not evidence that Mindwheel was released during this particular week.

worldAnchor.headline: TWA Flight 847 hijacked

bbsNote.headline: Commodore courts the household modem user
bbsNote.summary: June Gazette’s interview with Commodore’s Goheen puts cheaper telecomputing and service partnerships on the agenda.

posts.text: Goheen forecasts a Hayes-like smartmodem and an eventual price below $100, not an initial advertised purchase price.
The interview names service relationships and subscription snap packs; a possible Commodore service is an idea, not a launch.

curiosity.summary: Mindwheel blurs the bookshop and software shelf.
curiosity.detail: June Gazette describes Synapse electronic novels as hardback books with a disk at the back, with information in the printed book needed to play. Attribute to the June feature, not a release this week.

gadgetWatch.headline: Milton Bradley’s motorized robots await microcomputer interfaces
gadgetWatch.summary: PCW p.4 reports construction sets with educational BBC B experiments in Welsh schools using a control box. Milton Bradley was considering interface licences rather than launching its own interface. Expansion set about £20; largest set £60–£80.
